# Sjogren syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Connective tissue diseases > Sjogren syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/XP09WT)

---

## Summary

Sjogren syndrome is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease that most commonly occurs in middle-aged women. <u>Primary Sjogren syndrome</u> is <u>idiopathic</u>; Sjogren syndrome that occurs concomitantly with another autoimmune disease (e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, <u>systemic sclerosis</u>) is classified as <u>secondary Sjogren syndrome</u>. Sjogren syndrome most commonly manifests with <u>sicca syndrome</u> but can also manifest with systemic symptoms such as <u>arthritis</u>, <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>, and GI involvement as a result of <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltration of glandular and nonglandular organs. The diagnosis is confirmed by the detection of <u>autoantibodies</u> (<u>anti-Ro/SSA</u> or <u>anti-La/SSB antibodies</u>) in patients with <u>sicca syndrome</u>. <u>Salivary gland</u> <u>biopsy</u> is the <u>gold standard test</u> but is often only performed in patients with atypical presentations. Management focuses on supportive measures and, in patients with severe systemic disease, <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>.




![Sjogren syndrome fact sheet](media/d3jmazvu6z254vd5za5ed3ow.jpg)

Sjogren syndrome fact sheet

## Epidemiology

* Sex: : <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (∼ 9:1) [[1]](/library/FaXgm9)

* Age of onset: : typically 40–60 years [[1]](/library/FaXgm9)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Primary Sjogren syndrome</u>: <u>idiopathic</u> (association with <u>HLA</u>-DR52) [[2]](/library/DaX159)

* <u>Secondary Sjogren syndrome</u>: associated with another autoimmune disease, e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u>, <u>systemic sclerosis</u>, <u>polymyositis</u>, or <u>primary biliary cirrhosis</u> [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)





> [!TIP]
> Viral infections, e.g., <u>HCV</u>, <u>HIV</u>, <u>EBV</u>, and <u>HTLV</u>, are thought to be triggering factors for Sjogren syndrome; however, a causative relationship has not been established. [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)

---

## Clinical features

Clinical presentation varies widely, from isolated <u>sicca syndrome</u> to systemic involvement. See “Complications” for other clinical presentations.




### Sicca syndrome [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)[[4]](/library/CJaqwl)




* Ocular symptoms

* Xerophthalmia: dry eyes due to decreased secretion of tears (daily, persistent)

* <u>Keratoconjunctivitis sicca</u>

* <u>Conjunctival injection</u>

* <u>Eye</u> itching or burning sensation

* Blurred <u>vision</u>

* Recurrent sensation of sand or a foreign body in the eyes

* Oral symptoms

* Xerostomia: dry mouth due to decreased secretion of saliva (daily, persistent) which may lead to:  

* <u>Dental caries</u> and oral infections

* <u>Parotid gland</u> enlargement, often bilateral

* <u>Tongue</u> fissures

* Frequent need to drink liquids to aid <u>swallowing</u> and/or speaking

* Other glandular symptoms

* Vaginal dryness, leading to <u>dyspareunia</u> and an increased risk of infections

* Nasal dryness, leading to chronic <u>rhinitis</u> and <u>epistaxis</u>

* Pharyngeal, <u>tracheal</u>, and bronchial dryness, causing persistent dry <u>cough</u>

* Xerosis: abnormal <u>skin</u> dryness and <u>pruritus</u> (secondary to <u>hypohidrosis</u> or <u>anhidrosis</u>)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Xerostomia</u> and <u>xerophthalmia</u> are the classic symptoms of <u>sicca syndrome</u> and are present in ∼ 95% of patients with Sjogren syndrome. [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)[[5]](/library/WB1P-Q0)




![Tongue furrows](media/j8xhg2ysnbysxd6flqh66hci.jpg)

Tongue furrows




### Systemic disease  [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)[[4]](/library/CJaqwl)




* <u>Arthralgias</u> and/or <u>arthritis</u> (most common systemic symptom)

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>: <u>fever</u>, weight loss, fatigue

* GI involvement, e.g., <u>dysphagia</u> , <u>dyspepsia</u>, <u>reflux esophagitis</u>

* Pulmonary involvement: <u>interstitial lung disease</u>

* <u>Vasculitis</u> 

* Mainly cutaneous: palpable <u>purpura</u> in the legs, recurrent <u>urticaria</u>, <u>skin</u> <u>ulcerations</u>

* <u>Glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>Autoimmune thyroiditis</u>

* Neurological involvement, e.g., <u>peripheral neuropathy</u>, <u>myelitis</u>

* In patients with <u>secondary Sjogren syndrome</u>: features of a concomitant autoimmune condition, e.g., <u>malar rash</u> in patients with <u>SLE</u>





> [!TIP]
> Systemic symptoms are present in 50–60% of patients with Sjogren syndrome. [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[4]](/library/CJaqwl)[[6]](/library/VB1G-Q0)




* Consider Sjogren syndrome in patients with features of <u>sicca syndrome</u> without a known cause.

* The following are needed to confirm the diagnosis:

* Positive <u>anti-Ro/SSA</u> or <u>anti-La/SSB</u> <u>autoantibodies</u>

* Objective confirmation of <u>xerostomia</u> and <u>xerophthalmia</u>

* Classification criteria can help support the diagnosis.

* Further studies may be obtained depending on suspected organ involvement.





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)[[4]](/library/CJaqwl)




Obtain routine studies and <u>autoantibodies</u> for all patients. Prognostic markers may be ordered by a specialist.




* Routine studies: may show nonspecific supportive findings

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>normocytic anemia</u>, <u>leukopenia</u>, <u>eosinophilia</u>

* ↑ <u>ESR</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: <u>proteinuria</u> and/or <u>RBC casts</u> may indicate <u>glomerulonephritis</u> or <u>interstitial</u> nephritis

* <u>Autoantibodies</u>

* Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies ; (positive in ∼ 70% of cases) and anti-La/SSB antibodies;  (positive in ∼ 50% of cases):  target ribonucleoprotein <u>antigens</u> (Ro/La) in <u>epithelial</u> cells, especially in the <u>salivary glands</u> [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)

* <u>Antinuclear antibodies</u> (positive in up to 80% of cases) [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)

* <u>Rheumatoid factor</u> (positive in 50% of cases of <u>primary Sjogren syndrome</u>) [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)

* Prognostic markers: associated with a poor prognosis  

* <u>Cryoglobulinemia</u>

* <u>Hypergammaglobulinemia</u>

* ↓ <u>Complement C3</u> and/or C4





### Assessment of <u>xerostomia</u>




#### <u>Salivary gland</u> function studies [[5]](/library/WB1P-Q0)[[6]](/library/VB1G-Q0)[[7]](/library/QB1u0j0)




* Unstimulated salivary flow (preferred)

* Method: Saliva is collected for 5 minutes.

* Supportive finding: salivary flow ≤ 0.1 mL/minute [[6]](/library/VB1G-Q0)

* Alternative studies 

* Salivary <u>scintigraphy</u>

* Stimulated salivary flow





#### <u>Biopsy</u> of minor labial <u>salivary gland</u> [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)[[4]](/library/CJaqwl)




* <u>Gold standard test</u>, but not routinely required

* Consider if clinical presentation is atypical.

* Supportive findings

* Destruction of minor <u>salivary glands</u> (<u>fibrosis</u>, <u>parenchymal</u> <u>atrophy</u>)

* <u>Sialadenitis</u> with dense focal <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltrations





![Chronic sialadenitis in Sjogren syndrome](media/e3jwy7bo2vuhpdycnwteef0l.jpg)

Chronic sialadenitis in Sjogren syndrome




### Assessment of <u>xerophthalmia</u> [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)




* <u>Schirmer test</u>: shows decreased tear production

* <u>Slit lamp examination</u>

* <u>Tear film break-up time</u>: reduced (< 10 seconds)

* Ocular staining  

* Corneal <u>fluorescein stain</u>: punctate <u>epithelial</u> <u>erosions</u>

* <u>Conjunctival</u> lissamine green stain: <u>conjunctival</u> <u>erosions</u>





![Schirmer test](media/j7pxechoqkxgo5nf9410qz3s.jpg)

Schirmer test

![Punctate epithelial erosions](media/aufhy3vz4cyp2g8a0qj0gr0t.jpg)

Punctate epithelial erosions




### <u>Salivary gland</u> imaging studies [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)




May help determine <u>salivary gland</u> involvement and assess for complications (e.g., infections, <u>lymphoma</u>)




* <u>Ultrasound</u> of the <u>parotid gland</u>  

* May appear normal in early stages

* Alternating <u>hypoechoic</u> areas and band-like <u>hyperechoic</u> septa and cysts may be present in late stages.

* <u>MRI</u> of the <u>parotid gland</u>: The glandular <u>parenchyma</u> may have a honeycomb or cloud-like structure.





![Sjogren syndrome of the parotid gland](media/rt163qz9ql3f80n2ie1kwwan.jpg)

Sjogren syndrome of the parotid gland

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Iatrogenic</u>

* Chronic use of drugs, e.g., <u>antihistamines</u>, <u>antidepressants</u>, <u>anticholinergics</u>

* Head and neck radiation

* Corneal <u>surgery</u>, e.g., <u>LASIK</u>

* Systemic autoimmune diseases

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>IgG4-related disease</u>

* <u>Amyloidosis</u>

* Chronic viral infections

* <u>Hepatitis C</u>

* <u>HIV</u>

* <u>Atopic disease</u>: e.g., <u>allergic conjunctivitis</u>

* Other

* <u>Age-related sicca syndrome</u> [[8]](/library/H2WKQk0)

* Definition: <u>xerophthalmia</u> and <u>xerostomia</u> in older patients without evidence of Sjogren syndrome

* Etiology

* Decreased tear and saliva production (due to age-related <u>interstitial</u> <u>fibrosis</u>, acinar <u>atrophy</u> with fat replacement, ductal dilation, and nonspecific <u>chronic inflammation</u>)

* Decreased blinking rate

* Toxicity from topical drugs

* <u>Risk factors</u>: older age, female sex, medication use (e.g., <u>anticholinergics</u>)

* Clinical features: See “<u>Sicca syndrome</u>” above.

* Diagnostics: Consider in older patients with <u>sicca syndrome</u> and no evidence of underlying Sjogren syndrome. (See “Diagnostics” above.)

* <u>Dehydration</u>

* Uncontrolled <u>diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Graft-versus-host disease</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### General principles [[4]](/library/CJaqwl)[[5]](/library/WB1P-Q0)[[9]](/library/dB1o-Q0)




* Management should be guided by a rheumatologist and other specialists as required.

* Symptomatic <u>management of sicca syndrome</u> is the mainstay of treatment.

* For patients with active systemic disease, <u>immunosuppressants</u> may be considered.

* Monitor patients for the development of complications, e.g., <u>lymphoma</u>, and associated autoimmune diseases.





> [!TIP]
> Patients with Sjogren syndrome have an increased risk of developing <u>MALT lymphoma</u>.




### Management of sicca syndrome [[5]](/library/WB1P-Q0)[[9]](/library/dB1o-Q0)




#### <u>Xerostomia</u>




* All patients

* Frequent water intake

* <u>Caries</u> prophylaxis, e.g., regular dental hygienist visits, topical <u>fluoride</u> or <u>chlorhexidine</u>

* Avoidance of irritants (e.g., coffee, <u>alcohol</u>) and acidic beverages (e.g., herbal tea, cola) [[10]](/library/cZWa0P0)

* Artificial saliva

* Preferred treatment for patients without residual glandular function

* May be considered for all patients

* Patient with residual glandular function: stimulation of salivary flow

* First line: nonpharmacological stimulants, e.g., sugar-free lozenges or <u>gum</u>, acidic candy, xylitol

* Second line: oral <u>muscarinic agonists</u>

* Usually reserved for moderate or severe salivary dysfunction because of their potential adverse effects and the lack of strong evidence supporting their benefit

* Options: <u>pilocarpine</u>, <u>cevimeline</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Muscarinic agonists</u> are contraindicated in patients with <u>asthma</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>, and/or <u>glaucoma</u>. [[11]](/library/V-aGwM)




#### <u>Xerophthalmia</u> [[5]](/library/WB1P-Q0)[[9]](/library/dB1o-Q0)




Advise all patients to maintain adequate <u>eye</u> lubrication and avoid dry environments (e.g., shield eyes from wind, increase indoor <u>humidity</u>).




* First line: artificial tears for <u>volume replacement</u> and lubrication

* Second-line therapies: usually reserved for refractory or severe disease because of their potential adverse effects 

* Stimulation of <u>lacrimal gland</u> function with oral <u>muscarinic agonists</u>, i.e., <u>pilocarpine</u> or <u>cevimeline</u>

* Topical <u>immunosuppressive agents</u>, e.g., topical <u>cyclosporine</u>, short-term (2–4 weeks) topical <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* Serum <u>eye</u> drops





### Management of systemic disease [[5]](/library/WB1P-Q0)[[9]](/library/dB1o-Q0)




Management depends on the specific manifestation and should always be guided by a specialist.




* Inflammatory musculoskeletal <u>pain</u>

* <u>NSAIDs</u> or <u>acetaminophen</u>

* Low-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* DMARDS (e.g., <u>hydroxychloroquine</u>, <u>methotrexate</u>)

* Fatigue

* Regular exercise

* <u>Hydroxychloroquine</u> may be considered.  [[9]](/library/dB1o-Q0)

* Other manifestations of systemic disease : Systemic <u>immunosuppressants</u> (e.g., <u>glucocorticoids</u>, <u>cyclosporine</u>, <u>rituximab</u>) may be considered for severe symptoms.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>TNF-α inhibitors</u> can cause serious adverse effects (e.g., serious infections, <u>cytopenias</u>) and increase the risk of developing <u>non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u>, and therefore should be avoided in patients with Sjogren syndrome. [[9]](/library/dB1o-Q0)

---

## Complications

* Development of associated conditions

* Autoimmune diseases, e.g., <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u>, <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>B-cell lymphomas</u>, e.g., <u>MALT lymphoma</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u> ∼ 5% [[3]](/library/eB1x-Q0)

* Frequently manifests as unilateral, persistent <u>parotid</u> enlargement

* Predictors of <u>lymphoma</u> include <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, palpable <u>purpura</u>, and <u>cryoglobulinemia</u>.

* <u>Renal tubular acidosis type 1</u> [[12]](/library/YYXnn9)

* Corneal scarring, <u>ulcer</u>, rupture, and infection

* <u>Pregnancy</u>: fetal loss, <u>infant</u> with <u>neonatal lupus syndrome</u> and associated <u>complete heart block</u>





References:[[1]](/library/FaXgm9)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
